title: Depot injections, benzodiazepines and adherence
blurb: Offer long-acting injectables for the right reasons, give them safely, prescribe benzodiazepines with care and support adherence through shared decisions.
question: Marcus, 31, has had three relapses of schizophrenia after stopping his tablets. He says he forgets them and hates the weight gain. The team is considering a depot. What should guide the decision?

teach.body: A depot or long-acting injectable (LAI) antipsychotic is an intramuscular injection that releases medication over weeks. NICE CG178 says consider it for people who would prefer it after an acute episode, or where avoiding covert non-adherence (intentional or unintentional) is a clinical priority in the treatment plan. In plain English: a depot can help when tablets keep getting missed, but it should be the person's informed choice, not a punishment for 'non-compliance'.

teach.h: Is a depot a good option?

root.label: Doses being missed?
root.sub: Find the reason first, without judgement

children.label: Review drug or dose
children.sub: An LAI of the same drug keeps the side effect

steps.label: Same checks as oral
steps.sub: Benefits, side effects, baseline physical health

steps.label: Prescribe per BNF/SPC
steps.sub: Dose and interval titrated to response

teach.body: Check the prescription, product, dose, due date and site against the record. Ask about side effects since the last dose, especially movement problems such as akathisia, stiffness or tremor, and about weight, sleep and sexual function. Oily depots are given by deep intramuscular injection, aspirating before injecting and alternating sites, as the product's SPC states; many trusts also teach a Z-track technique, but that comes from local training, not the SPCs. Record the batch, site and next due date, and act on missed appointments promptly.
teach.cite: CG178 1.3.6.4; depot SPCs (for example Depixol, Haldol Decanoate, Clopixol); local policy

head: Issue
Guidance
rows: Can occur with short-term or prolonged use (MHRA Jan 2026)
Agree a plan for reducing and ending treatment
Tailored dose reduction; avoid abrupt cessation
Not offered except short-term in a crisis (CG113)

teach.body: CG178 says the choice of antipsychotic is made by the person and professional together, discussing metabolic, extrapyramidal, cardiovascular, hormonal and other side effects, and recording which side effects the person is most willing to tolerate. Ask about adherence non-judgementally and find the reason: forgetting, side effects, beliefs or practical barriers. NICE says do not offer 'adherence therapy' as a specific intervention; address the actual reasons instead.

His care coordinator, Nurse Reid, explores why tablets get missed: forgetting and weight gain. She explains the depot options, including second-generation LAIs with fewer movement side effects, and discusses weight effects of each. Marcus chooses a depot that he feels better about, with clinic appointments near his work. They agree physical health monitoring, a plan for missed appointments and a review of how he feels on it.

teach.text: A depot is not a way round consent. Without legal authority (for example MHA Part 4 for a detained patient) a capable person can refuse it. And benzodiazepine dependence is not just a long-term problem: MHRA warns it can develop with short-term use too.

items: Consider an LAI if the person prefers it or avoiding covert non-adherence is a priority.
Choose with the person: preferences, side effects, practicalities; prescribe per BNF/SPC.
At each depot: check details, ask about side effects, record site and next due date.
Benzodiazepines: plan the ending before starting, avoid abrupt stopping, beware opioids.
Find the reason for non-adherence; shared decisions, not 'compliance' pressure.

summary: You can now explain when a depot antipsychotic is appropriate and give it safely. You can apply current benzodiazepine safety advice and support adherence through shared decision-making.

A.q: According to NICE CG178, when should a depot antipsychotic be considered?
options: For every person admitted under section 3 of the MHA
When the person prefers it after an acute episode
When oral tablets cost more than the injection
For anyone aged over 65 who has schizophrenia
A.why: CG178 1.5.5.3: consider a depot for people who would prefer it after an acute episode, or where avoiding covert non-adherence is a clinical priority.

whyNot.0: Detention status is not the NICE criterion for a depot.
whyNot.2: Cost comparison is not a CG178 reason to choose a depot.
whyNot.3: Age is not a criterion for depot treatment.

A.q: Which statement about benzodiazepine dependence reflects MHRA advice from January 2026?
options: It occurs after at least 6 months of use
It occurs in people with a substance misuse history
It can occur with short-term or prolonged use
It is prevented by taking the dose at night
A.why: MHRA (Jan 2026): addiction and dependence can occur with short-term or prolonged treatment; warnings on dependence, withdrawal and tolerance were strengthened.

whyNot.0: Dependence is not limited to 6 months or more of use.
whyNot.1: A substance misuse history raises risk, but anyone can become dependent.
whyNot.3: Night-time dosing does not prevent dependence.

A.q: Why is prescribing a benzodiazepine with an opioid a particular concern?
options: It risks fatal respiratory depression
It commonly causes serotonin toxicity
It blocks the opioid's pain-relieving effect
It causes severe neutropenia
A.why: MHRA (Mar 2020): co-prescribing benzodiazepines with opioids can cause additive CNS depression, sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death.

whyNot.2: Benzodiazepines do not block opioid analgesia.
whyNot.3: Neutropenia is the classic clozapine risk.

B.q: Deborah, 44, attends for her depot. She paces, cannot sit still and says she feels restless inside since the last dose. What should the nurse do?
options: Give the depot and suggest relaxation exercises
Record it as anxiety and continue as planned
Hold the depot and report suspected akathisia
Give the depot with a PRN benzodiazepine
B.why: Inner restlessness and pacing after an antipsychotic dose suggests akathisia, an extrapyramidal side effect; CG178 1.3.6.4 notes it overlaps with agitation and must be monitored. Report before giving more.

whyNot.0: Relaxation does not address a medication side effect.
whyNot.1: Akathisia can be mistaken for anxiety; recording it as anxiety misses it.
whyNot.3: Adding a benzodiazepine without review masks the side effect.

B.q: Tariq, 52, has taken diazepam for 9 months and wants to stop. What is the best approach?
options: Stop it today, as diazepam is long-acting
Agree a tailored, gradual reduction plan
Switch to zopiclone and stop that next month
Reduce by half each week until stopped
B.why: MHRA (Jan 2026): provide an individually tailored dose reduction schedule, counsel on withdrawal and avoid abrupt cessation, with regular support.

whyNot.0: Abrupt stopping risks withdrawal, whatever the half-life.
whyNot.2: Z-drugs carry the same dependence warnings.
whyNot.3: A fixed fast schedule is not individually tailored.

B.q: Lena, 28, has panic disorder and asks her GP for lorazepam to take long term. What does NICE CG113 advise?
options: Lorazepam taken daily for up to 12 months
Lorazepam when attacks occur, long term
Lorazepam alongside an SSRI for 6 months
Benzodiazepines should not be prescribed
B.why: CG113 1.3.20: benzodiazepines are associated with a less good outcome in the long term and should not be prescribed for panic disorder.

whyNot.0: Long-term daily use is against NICE advice for panic disorder.
whyNot.1: PRN long-term use is still benzodiazepine treatment for panic.
whyNot.2: NICE does not recommend combining a benzodiazepine for panic disorder.

C.q: Jamal, 26, misses his oral antipsychotic about half the time. He says the tablets make him 'feel like a zombie'. Which response best reflects NICE CG178?
options: Explore side effects and review options together
Refer him for a structured course of adherence therapy
Tell him a depot will be given if he misses more
Ask his family to watch him take each tablet
C.why: CG178 1.3.5.1 and 1.3.6.3: choose medication together, discuss side effects and record which are tolerable. CG178 1.4.4.7 says do not offer adherence therapy as a specific intervention.

whyNot.1: NICE advises against adherence therapy as a specific intervention.
whyNot.2: Threatening a depot is coercive and ignores the cause.
whyNot.3: Supervision by family does not address the side effect driving non-adherence.

C.q: Sandra, 49, informal and with capacity, attends the depot clinic and says she does not want today's injection. She is well. What should the nurse do?
options: Give it, as it is prescribed and is due today
Give it, as missing a dose risks a relapse
Respect her decision, explore why, tell the team
Arrange for her to be detained so it can be given
C.why: A capable informal patient can refuse treatment. The nurse respects the decision, explores reasons such as side effects, discusses risks, documents and informs the prescriber and care coordinator.

whyNot.0: A prescription is not consent; giving it would be treatment without legal authority.
whyNot.1: Relapse risk does not override a capable person's refusal.
whyNot.3: Detention needs MHA criteria; a well person declining a dose does not meet them.

C.q: Ken, 60, takes methadone and has been started on diazepam for anxiety after a bereavement. Which advice is most important?
options: Take both together at night for the best effect
Get urgent help if very sleepy or breathing slowly
Double the diazepam dose if anxiety becomes severe
Stop the methadone while taking the diazepam
C.why: MHRA (2020): benzodiazepines with opioids risk fatal respiratory depression; with methadone the effect may be delayed, so monitor for at least 2 weeks and tell the person to seek urgent help for sedation or breathing problems.

whyNot.0: Timing them together does not reduce the respiratory risk.
whyNot.2: Increasing the dose raises the risk of respiratory depression.
whyNot.3: Stopping methadone abruptly is unsafe and not the advice.

reteach.title: Choice, safety, honesty
reteach.question: How do you support someone with medication they find hard to take?

blocks.body: Missing medication has reasons: side effects, forgetting, beliefs, practical barriers. A depot suits people who prefer it or where covert non-adherence matters. Benzodiazepines need an exit plan from the start. Every choice is made with the person.

blocks.text: A depot does not remove the need for consent or legal authority.

explain.body: The person prefers it after an acute episode, or avoiding covert non-adherence is a clinical priority. Consider preferences, attitudes to injections, and practical issues such as home visits and clinic location.

test.q: What practical factor does CG178 say to consider when starting a depot?
options: The ward's injection budget
The nurse's preferred injection site
The person's date of diagnosis
Home visits and clinic location
test.why: CG178 1.5.6.1: take into account preferences, attitudes to regular IM injections and organisational procedures such as home visits and clinic location.

whyNot.0: Budgets are not the CG178 factor.
whyNot.1: The site follows the product SPC and the person's needs.
whyNot.2: Diagnosis date is not a factor named in CG178.

explain.body: First-generation depots cause extrapyramidal reactions more often; second-generation depots (aripiprazole, paliperidone, risperidone, olanzapine embonate) less often. Ask about movement problems, weight and other effects at each visit.

test.q: Compared with first-generation depots, second-generation depots are associated with what?
options: More extrapyramidal reactions
Fewer extrapyramidal reactions
No metabolic side effects
No need for physical monitoring
test.why: BNF: extrapyramidal reactions occur less frequently with second-generation depot preparations.

whyNot.2: Second-generation drugs can cause metabolic effects.
whyNot.3: Physical monitoring applies to all antipsychotics.

explain.body: Dependence can occur with short-term or prolonged use. Plan the ending before starting; tailored reductions; avoid abrupt cessation. Fatal respiratory depression risk with opioids. Not for GAD except short-term crisis; not for panic disorder.

test.q: When should a plan for reducing and ending a benzodiazepine be discussed?
options: After 4 weeks of treatment
When the person asks to stop
Before treatment is started
If tolerance develops
test.why: MHRA (Jan 2026): discuss plans for reducing or ending treatment before initiation.

whyNot.0: MHRA advises planning before starting, not later.
whyNot.1: Waiting for the person to ask delays planning.
whyNot.3: Planning should come before any tolerance develops.

explain.body: Decide medication together, discuss side effects and record those the person will tolerate. Ask about adherence regularly and non-judgementally. NICE does not recommend adherence therapy as a specific intervention in psychosis.

test.q: Which side effects does CG178 say to discuss when choosing an antipsychotic?
options: Metabolic, movement, cardiac and hormonal
Hepatic, renal, dermatological and dental
Hearing, vision, balance and taste
Bleeding, clotting, bruising and anaemia
test.why: CG178 1.3.5.1: discuss metabolic, extrapyramidal, cardiovascular, hormonal and other side effects such as unpleasant subjective experiences.

whyNot.1: These are not the categories CG178 lists.
